alalal-e86561-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 5: whether an article is something complex or incomplex.

alalal-e86561-d1e113.summary: States the second problem: what an article is in reality, complex or incomplex.

alalal-e86561-d1e122.summary: Proposes that an article is incomplex, such as 'the passion' or 'the resurrection'.

alalal-e86561-d1e132.summary: First argument: faith is a simple light (Dionysius), so it concerns what is simple, not complex.

alalal-e86561-d1e143.summary: Second argument: there is no complexity in God, and articles are about God.

alalal-e86561-d1e152.summary: Third argument: an article is defined as an indivisible truth, and nothing complex is indivisible.

alalal-e86561-d1e163.summary: Fourth argument: if articles were enunciables, time would belong to their essence, so 'Christ suffered at instant A' and 'at B' would be different articles.

alalal-e86561-d1e183.summary: Further: if a determinate time belonged to the article, Augustine's saying that times have changed but faith remains unchanged would be false, and moderns and ancients would not share the same faith.

alalal-e86561-d1e203.summary: Sed contra: consent is only to something complex, and faith is consent (Damascene), so an article is complex.

alalal-e86561-d1e222.summary: Second sed contra: if incomplex, Jews who believe in the incarnation as future would believe the same article we believe as past.

alalal-e86561-d1e233.summary: Third sed contra: if simple, one who believed in Christ's incarnation but not that Christ has become incarnate would not be a heretic; since that is false, the article is an enunciable, not a thing.

alalal-e86561-d1e249.summary: Fourth, against the enunciable view: Cornelius did not believe that Christ had become incarnate, yet his alms and prayers were heard, which requires faith; and if he did believe it, Peter was sent to preach to him in vain.

alalal-e86561-d1e278.summary: Solution, without prejudice: a determinate time is not of the essence of the articles, but a certain complexity is. In every article divine truth underlies, determined by what belongs to essence and persons and by its effects in restoring nature and grace. We can signify this determination only by composition, though in itself it is immediate, as whiteness is in a surface without medium yet we signify it with a mark of composition. So the determinant in the determined is supposed in the article, but the mark of composition added by the signifying soul, which essentially includes a determinate time, is not of its essence.
claims: An article is a complex reality but not a time-bound proposition.
Divine truth underlies every article, determined by essence, persons and saving effects.

alalal-e86561-d1e339.summary: Reply to the first argument: though faith's light is simple, it inclines to consent, so it requires complexity in the article, but not that which makes an enunciable with a determinate time.

alalal-e86561-d1e355.summary: Reply to the second: though there is no real complexity in God, some articles are complex in mode of signifying, as 'God is three and one', others because of diverse effects, others because of the nature united to Christ.

alalal-e86561-d1e376.summary: Reply to the third: an article is called indivisible truth because the division of credibles stops at it, not because it is wholly incomplex.

alalal-e86561-d1e387.summary: Reply to the fourth: in Albert's judgment the enunciable is not the article, but the complex thing ordered to every time.
claims: The article is a complex reality indifferent to time, not an enunciable.
concepts: res complexa ordinata ad omne tempus

alalal-e86561-d1e396.summary: Reply to the sed contra: consent seeks only a complex thing, on which it imposes a mode of composition determined by the truth assented to; though true in the thing, the composition is in the soul as its maker (Metaphysics VI).

alalal-e86561-d1e418.summary: Reply to the second and third sed contra: we must believe not only the article but what has been determined about the articles by the Apostles' preaching; these concern faith from hearing, and much, including determination of time, has accrued to faith by hearing and preaching, though not of the articles' substance.
claims: Determinations of time come to faith through preaching, not from the substance of the articles.

alalal-e86561-d1e442.summary: This also answers the next objection.

alalal-e86561-d1e447.summary: Reply on Cornelius: when the time was not yet determined by the ages of the world, prophecy or apostolic preaching, some could relate to any time indeterminately; now it is not so, since the time is determined by the course of the ages, Daniel's prophecy, and the preaching that has gone out to all the earth.
claims: Before the time of the incarnation was proclaimed, faith in it could be indeterminate as to time; now it must be determinate.

alalal-e86561.summary: Article 5 asks whether an article of faith is complex or incomplex in reality. Arguments for incomplexity cite faith's simple light, divine simplicity, indivisibility, and the unity of faith across times. Arguments for complexity hold that consent is only to the complex and that otherwise one could not distinguish Jewish from Christian belief or identify heresy. Albert holds, without prejudice, that an article is a complex reality but not a time-bound proposition. Divine truth underlies every article, determined by essence, persons and saving effects. We can signify that determination only by composition, but the mark of composition, with its determinate time, belongs to the signifying soul, not to the article. Determinations of time come to faith through apostolic preaching. Before they were proclaimed, as in Cornelius' case, belief could be indeterminate about time; now it cannot.
claims: An article of faith is a complex reality ordered to all times, not a time-bound enunciable.
The temporal composition of an article belongs to the signifying mind, not to the article.
Determinations of time in faith come through preaching and bind once proclaimed.
